title: Polio Surveillance and Vaccination amid a cVDPV2 Upsurge During the 2026 Bundibugyo Virus Disease Response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
content: Introduction: The 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo coincided with the international poliovirus emergency and a national upsurge of circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2). This study examined support between the BVD response and the polio programme, acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) surveillance and polio campaigns. Methods: This retrospective study analysed 174 BVD situation reports (data to 12 November 2026), 14 weekly polio bulletins (weeks 31–45) and other official sources. We compared provincial non-polio AFP rates and stool adequacy for weeks 1–45 of 2025 and 2026 across bulletin editions, assessed 2026 indicators against programme benchmarks, and extracted silent health zones, cVDPV2 AFP cases, programme support and campaign evidence (plans, local activity or published results). Results: By 12 November, eight provinces had reported 11,254 confirmed BVD cases, 94.3% in Ituri and North Kivu. Reported cVDPV2 AFP cases in 2026 rose from 25 on 6 August to 98, against nine in 2025; three were in BVD-affected South Kivu and North Ubangi. Bulletins listed polio-team support in six provinces, and BVD responders supported Tshopo's polio campaign launch. All eight BVD provinces met the detection benchmark, but North and South Kivu had higher detection and lower stool adequacy than in 2025 in 13 of 14 editions, and notification within seven days was below 80% in four provinces. All four health zones without AFP notification for 12 months were in Ituri and North Kivu. Laboratory receipt within three days was 0–10% in BVD provinces and 13.8% nationally. Ituri, North Kivu and South Kivu were absent from the May–June campaign results; September results for the two Kivus appeared eight weeks after the round, with none for Ituri's planned round. Conclusion: AFP detection was maintained in BVD-affected provinces, but late notification, lower stool adequacy in the Kivu provinces, silent zones in the outbreak epicentre and nationwide transport delays left gaps as reported cVDPV2 cases rose. Health-zone records and timely campaign reporting would help track continuity during concurrent emergencies.
